tasks.prompt: Some people prefer several smaller local information points. Others prefer a large central public information centre. Write four paragraphs about both views and give your own opinion. Include reasons and a concrete example.

People have different preferences about public service locations. Some prefer several smaller local information points, but others favour a large central public information centre. I think the decision should consider the purpose and the people involved.

On the one hand, local information points reduce the journey needed to ask a basic question. A resident can visit a familiar place near home. For example, a community centre helps someone find the correct office for a service and explains which contact details to use.

On the other hand, a central centre can bring several specialists together and offer longer opening hours. Small locations need staff, space and updated materials. A visitor may still need referral elsewhere for a detailed question. Spreading resources too thinly can make each location less useful.

Taking both views into account, I support local help for common questions and central support for complex ones. Staff should know how to connect people with the right service.

People have different preferences about campus transport. Some prefer more campus shuttle services, but others favour more parking spaces for private vehicles. I think the decision should consider the purpose and the people involved.

On the one hand, a reliable shuttle gives students another way to reach campus without a private vehicle. Several people can share one journey. For example, a nursing student travels between a station and the school with books and a uniform without arranging a separate ride every day.

On the other hand, a shuttle route cannot match every student's timetable or starting point. Early placements and late activities may require different arrangements. Parking also matters for some people with access needs. A transport plan should consider reliability and accessibility instead of assuming one option fits all journeys.

To sum up, I support useful shuttle routes alongside appropriate access arrangements. The best investment depends on the journeys students actually need to make.

On the other hand, not everyone can cycle, and distance, weather or mobility needs can make it impractical. Pedestrians and bus passengers also need safe, accessible routes. A new bicycle rack alone does not solve a difficult junction. Transport spending needs to consider the full journey and a range of users.

On balance, I support bicycle improvements within a wider access plan. Walking, public transport and individual access needs should remain part of the decision.

People have different preferences about library collections. Some prefer more electronic nursing books, but others favour more printed nursing books. I think the decision should consider the purpose and the people involved.

On the one hand, an electronic book can be accessed without carrying a heavy volume. Search tools help a student find a familiar term quickly. For example, a learner checks a course reading from a dormitory desk after returning from a placement, provided the library licence allows access.

On the other hand, printed books work without a charged device and offer a different reading experience. Digital licences may limit simultaneous users or require a connection. Some students find long screen reading uncomfortable. The availability of a title in digital form does not guarantee that everyone can use it easily.

Taking both views into account, I prefer a mixture based on course demand and accessibility. Students should know which format is available before an assignment deadline.

People have different preferences about course materials costs. Some prefer free open course materials, but others favour a required published textbook. I think the decision should consider the purpose and the people involved.

On the one hand, free materials reduce the cost of joining a course. Students can open the same reading without waiting to buy a book. For example, a teacher shares an openly available language worksheet and clearly explains the source, so everyone can prepare for the next lesson.

On the other hand, a published textbook may provide a carefully organised sequence and useful teacher resources. Free material still needs review for accuracy, level and permission to reuse it. A collection of unrelated pages can be confusing. Price alone does not establish the quality of a learning resource.

To sum up, I support free materials when they meet the course goals. Teachers should explain how the readings fit together and offer clear guidance.

People have different preferences about writing assistance tools. Some prefer trying a personal revision before using a tool, but others favour using digital writing suggestions immediately. I think the decision should consider the purpose and the people involved.

On balance, I prefer a first attempt and a short self-check before tool support. Students should explain accepted changes and follow course rules.

Taking both views into account, I prefer a shared component and a clear individual component. Students should understand both before the project begins.

Unlimited flexibility also creates confusion, so students need a clear request process. Fairness does not always mean treating different situations as identical.

To sum up, I support normal deadlines with a transparent process for reasonable adjustments. The learning goal and the timing of feedback should guide decisions.

On balance, I support a few affordable core meals with some rotating choices. Students should be able to find suitable information before buying.

People have different preferences about student travel programmes. Some prefer short study visits overseas, but others favour international learning activities at home. I think the decision should consider the purpose and the people involved.

A participant learns to ask practical questions in an unfamiliar place. For example, a nursing student joins an approved campus visit and compares classroom arrangements with those at home.

On the other hand, travel requires money, time and careful planning. Some students cannot leave work or family responsibilities. International guests and online exchanges can also offer useful perspectives at home. A short visit does not automatically give a full understanding of another country's professional system.

Taking both views into account, I support overseas opportunities alongside accessible local alternatives. Students need clear learning goals and realistic information about costs.

For example, a graduate explains how they organised language practice and which questions are useful before starting. On the other hand, one person's experience may not match current requirements or another student's circumstances. Formal licensing and immigration information can change. Official sources are needed for those rules. Personal stories are useful examples, but they should not become promises about a student's future route.

To sum up, I prefer official information for requirements and alumni stories for practical perspective. Students should keep the two purposes clear.

People have different preferences about hospital staff spaces. Some prefer protecting a dedicated staff break area, but others favour using available rooms mainly for work activities. I think the decision should consider the purpose and the people involved.

On the one hand, a separate break area gives staff somewhere to step away from active work during an authorised break. Colleagues can sit down and have a meal in an appropriate space. For example, a clearly designated room avoids using a busy corridor for ordinary break activities.

On the other hand, hospital space has many competing uses, and some departments need more rooms for essential work. A break room also needs suitable access and maintenance. An attractive room alone does not ensure that staff can take breaks. Work arrangements and local rules remain part of the discussion.

On balance, I support protected break space alongside careful planning of clinical space. The decision should include the people using both areas.

People have different preferences about clinical teaching groups. Some prefer smaller clinical teaching groups, but others favour larger groups for shared explanations. I think the decision should consider the purpose and the people involved.

On the other hand, small groups require more teaching time and suitable space. Some general explanations can be shared effectively with a larger class. Taking both views into account, I prefer larger sessions for common information and smaller supervised groups for practice. The teaching goal should determine the format.

tasks.prompt: Some people prefer a regular volunteer commitment. Others prefer occasional volunteer events. Write four paragraphs about both views and give your own opinion. Include reasons and a concrete example.
tasks.zh: 主題：長期志工與短期活動。練習比較兩種做法：開頭交代選擇，兩個主體段各寫理由及具體例子，結尾說自己的選擇。共四段，至少150字；這是意見練習，不是現行機構規定。
tasks.sample:
People have different preferences about volunteer programmes. Some prefer a regular volunteer commitment, but others favour occasional volunteer events. I think the decision should consider the purpose and the people involved.

On the one hand, regular volunteering can help a student understand a community organisation over time. The learner becomes familiar with the agreed role and schedule. For example, a student helps at a non-clinical information event each month and gradually learns how the team organises its materials. An organisation can describe the task, time commitment and supervision before recruiting.

On the other hand, a long commitment may not fit changing course and placement schedules. Occasional events allow more people to take part. Volunteers also need training and a role within their abilities. Attendance alone is not a reason to ask a student to perform tasks outside that role.

To sum up, I support both regular and occasional volunteering with clear responsibilities. Participation should fit the student's timetable and the organisation's needs.

tasks.prompt: Some people prefer reading research articles in a guided group. Others prefer starting with short research summaries. Write four paragraphs about both views and give your own opinion. Include reasons and a concrete example.
tasks.zh: 主題：研究讀書會與短篇摘要。練習比較兩種做法：開頭交代選擇，兩個主體段各寫理由及具體例子，結尾說自己的選擇。共四段，至少150字；這是意見練習，不是現行機構規定。
tasks.sample:
People have different preferences about student research access. Some prefer reading research articles in a guided group, but others favour starting with short research summaries. I think the decision should consider the purpose and the people involved.

On the one hand, a guided group can show students how a research article is organised. Learners ask where a claim comes from and how the study was described. For example, a teacher helps the group locate the research question and separate the authors' findings from their wider discussion.

On the other hand, a full article can contain unfamiliar methods and difficult vocabulary. Beginners may spend all their time translating without understanding the purpose. A clear summary can provide a starting point, but it may leave out limitations. The difficulty needs to fit the teaching support available.

On balance, I prefer accessible summaries followed by selected parts of full articles. Students can gradually take on more detailed reading with guidance.

People have different preferences about community events timing. Some prefer evening community information events, but others favour daytime community information events. I think the decision should consider the purpose and the people involved.

On the one hand, evening events may be easier for people with ordinary daytime work or classes. A family can attend after returning home. For example, a community centre offers a general service-information session after dinner and leaves time for visitors to ask practical questions. On the other hand, evenings do not suit everyone. Some people work at night, care for family members or have limited transport after dark. Staff and venues also have opening restrictions. Daytime sessions can be more convenient for other groups. One time slot cannot represent the whole community.

Taking both views into account, I prefer a varied schedule and clear information in more than one format. Organisers should ask the intended audience about access.

tasks.zh: 主題：綠地與新教室。這題練「全部統一規定」和「保留個人選擇」的差別，不能只列出兩種工具。四段寫支持共同規則的理由、規則的限制與例子，再表明立場；至少150字。
tasks.sample:
There is a debate about whether more quiet outdoor spaces on campus should become the standard choice. Some people want one common approach, but others prefer more flexibility. I think a clear plan needs to respect different circumstances.

On the one hand, supporters of a common approach see useful benefits. Outdoor spaces give students a place for informal conversation or a short break between activities. A shaded seating area can also support small non-clinical group discussions. For example, students review an English dialogue together outside before returning to the library for individual work.

On the other hand, a single rule does not fit every situation. Teaching rooms are necessary for scheduled classes and suitable equipment. A growing course may struggle to find space at busy times. Weather also limits the use of outdoor areas. The value of a green space needs consideration alongside the practical requirements of the learning programme.

All things considered, I support protecting useful outdoor areas while reviewing how existing classrooms are used. New construction should answer a clear need.

tasks.prompt: Some people prefer sharing study notes with classmates. Others prefer keeping individual notes until personal review is complete. Write four paragraphs about both views and give your own opinion. Include reasons and a concrete example.
tasks.zh: 主題：共用筆記與個人筆記。練習比較兩種做法：開頭交代選擇，兩個主體段各寫理由及具體例子，結尾說自己的選擇。共四段，至少150字；這是意見練習，不是現行機構規定。
tasks.sample:
People have different preferences about shared learning resources. Some prefer sharing study notes with classmates, but others favour keeping individual notes until personal review is complete. I think the decision should consider the purpose and the people involved.

On the one hand, shared notes can help classmates notice a missing point or compare explanations. A learner can ask why another person organised a topic differently. For example, two nursing students compare an outline after class and check an uncertain detail against the approved course material.

On the other hand, personal notes may contain mistakes or shorthand that another person misunderstands. Copying a complete set can also replace the work of thinking through the lesson. Students need to respect course rules and avoid sharing confidential material. A large folder of notes is not automatically a reliable learning resource.

On balance, I prefer voluntary sharing after personal review, with sources clearly identified. Classmates should discuss questions rather than simply copy one another's pages.

tasks.prompt: Some people think that hospitals should be free for everyone. Others think patients should pay for their own treatment. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
tasks.zh: 有人認為醫院應該對所有人免費，有人認為病人應自付。討論兩種看法並提出你的意見。
tasks.sample:
People have different opinions about who should pay for hospital care. Some believe hospitals should be free for everyone, while others think patients should pay for their own treatment. In my opinion, basic hospital care should be free, but patients can share a small part of the cost.

On the one hand, there are strong reasons to make hospitals free. Illness is often not a person's fault, and a serious disease can cost more than a family earns in a year. If treatment is expensive, poor people may wait too long before they see a doctor, and a small problem can become a dangerous one. Free care also protects the whole society, because people with infectious diseases are more likely to get treatment early.

On the other hand, some people argue that patients should pay for their own treatment. Hospitals need a lot of money for staff, equipment and medicine, and if everything is free, more public money would be needed, which could mean higher taxes. They also believe that when services cost nothing, some people use them too often, for example by going to the emergency room for a minor cold. This makes waiting times longer for patients who really need help.

In my view, the best system combines both ideas. The government should pay for most hospital treatment, especially for serious illnesses, children and older people. At the same time, a small fee for each visit can stop people from using hospitals when they do not need to.

In conclusion, health care should not depend on how much money a person has, but a fair shared system is more realistic than completely free hospitals.

tasks.prompt: Many young people today spend several hours a day on their phones. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to solve them?
tasks.zh: 現在很多年輕人每天花好幾小時滑手機。這造成什麼問題？可以怎麼解決？
tasks.sample:
Nowadays, many young people spend several hours a day on their phones. Although smartphones are useful, using them too much can cause serious problems. This essay will discuss these problems and suggest some solutions.

The first problem is health. Young people who look at their screens late at night often sleep less, and poor sleep makes it harder to concentrate at school. Sitting for hours also means less exercise, and some teenagers develop neck and eye pain. The second problem is social. When friends spend a meal looking at their own phones, they talk less face to face, and some young people feel lonely even though they are always online. Finally, social media can affect mental health, because users often compare their lives with the perfect photos they see.

There are several ways to deal with these problems. First, young people can use the screen-time tools that most phones already have, such as daily limits and a sleep mode that turns off notifications at night. Second, schools can teach students how social media apps are designed to keep them scrolling, so that they can make better choices. Third, families can create simple rules, for example no phones at the dinner table, and parents should follow the same rules.

To conclude, spending too much time on phones can harm young people's health and their relationships with friends and family. However, with personal limits, education at school and support from families, young people can enjoy the benefits of their phones without letting the phones control their lives.

tasks.prompt: Some people believe that the best way to improve public health is to increase the number of sports facilities. Others think other measures are more effective. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
tasks.zh: 有人認為改善大眾健康最好的方法是增加運動設施，也有人認為其他方法更有效。你同意到什麼程度？
tasks.sample:
Some people believe that building more sports facilities is the best way to improve public health, while others think that other measures work better. I partly agree that sports facilities are helpful, but I believe they are not the most effective solution on their own.

It is true that sports facilities can make people healthier. When there is a park, a swimming pool or a basketball court near their home, people are more likely to exercise regularly. Regular exercise lowers the risk of heart disease, diabetes and obesity, and it can also reduce stress. Free or cheap facilities are especially important for families who cannot pay for a gym.

However, facilities alone do not change people's habits. Many people are too busy or too tired to exercise after work, and some do not know why exercise matters. In addition, public health depends on more than exercise. A healthy diet, clean air, regular health checks and not smoking are just as important. For example, a city with many gyms will still have health problems if fast food is cheaper than vegetables or if people cannot afford to see a doctor early.

For these reasons, I think governments should use several measures together. They can build sports facilities, but they should also teach healthy eating at school, put clear labels on unhealthy food, offer free health checks and support people who want to quit smoking.

Overall, more sports facilities are a good step, but public health improves most when exercise is combined with education, prevention and healthy food choices.

tasks.prompt: Some people support studying in a small group, while others favour studying alone. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
tasks.zh: 主題：讀書會與自己讀書。討論兩種看法並表達自己的意見。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
People have different views about study groups. Some support studying in a small group, while others prefer studying alone. In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. Group members explain difficult ideas to one another. A student notices a missing step during a practice explanation, so the speaker checks the textbook again. For example, three classmates compare their notes after a lesson. Each person brings a different question to the meeting.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. Studying alone gives a learner control over the pace. One student needs extra time for English vocabulary, but another already knows those words. A group sometimes moves too quickly or spends the whole meeting discussing one person's difficulty. Quiet individual review also avoids unnecessary conversation.

A practical response should connect these arguments with the way the service or course actually works. A school can provide a room and a list of discussion questions without making every meeting compulsory. Students can bring one prepared answer and one question. The teacher can also offer a separate way to ask for help. This arrangement includes learners with different timetables.

All things considered, I prefer a short group meeting after individual preparation. Both activities have a clear purpose, so neither one needs to replace the other. A useful decision weighs the benefits against the limitations and explains how people with different circumstances can take part.

tasks.prompt: Some people argue that studying in a small group should completely replace studying alone. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
tasks.zh: 主題：讀書會與自己讀書。同意程度題：先表明是否贊成把規定套用在所有情況，理由要支持同一立場。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
Some people argue that studying in a small group should completely replace studying alone. This proposal raises questions about study groups. I disagree with applying it as a universal rule. There are useful ideas behind the proposal, but different situations require a more flexible approach.

It is reasonable to recognise the benefits of studying in a small group. Group members explain difficult ideas to one another. A student notices a missing step during a practice explanation, so the speaker checks the textbook again. For example, three classmates compare their notes after a lesson. Each person brings a different question to the meeting.

Nevertheless, a decision must also take account of the other side. Studying alone gives a learner control over the pace. One student needs extra time for English vocabulary, but another already knows those words. A group sometimes moves too quickly or spends the whole meeting discussing one person's difficulty. Quiet individual review also avoids unnecessary conversation.

For these reasons, I favour clear guidance with practical alternatives rather than a single requirement for everyone. A school can provide a room and a list of discussion questions without making every meeting compulsory. Students can bring one prepared answer and one question. The teacher can also offer a separate way to ask for help. This arrangement includes learners with different timetables.

On balance, I prefer a short group meeting after individual preparation. Both activities have a clear purpose, so neither one needs to replace the other. This is why I do not support the proposal as a universal rule. A decision should respond to real needs and preserve a workable route for different people.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring using recorded lectures for review over attending every review session in person. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?
tasks.zh: 主題：課堂錄影與現場聽課。分析優點和缺點；題目沒有要求哪邊較多，不必硬選輸贏。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
The proposal favouring using recorded lectures for review over attending every review session in person raises questions about lecture recordings. This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. A recording allows a student to listen to an explanation again. A learner can pause at an unfamiliar word and look it up. For example, a nursing student reviews a lesson after an early placement day and writes down two questions for the next class.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. A live review session gives students a chance to ask questions immediately. The teacher notices confusion and explains an idea in a different way. A recording alone does not answer a new question. Students also need a quiet place and a suitable device to use recordings.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. Teachers can provide a short written outline with each recording. This supports students with limited internet access and makes the key points easier to find. A weekly question session adds interaction. The plan should explain which activities need attendance and which ones can be reviewed at home.

To sum up, I support recordings as an extra resource. Live opportunities to ask questions should remain available, especially for difficult practical topics. The advantages are most useful when the limitations are acknowledged and there is a practical alternative for people who need it.

tasks.prompt: Institutions promote using recorded lectures for review, but some people find this approach difficult to use or fit into their routine. What problems can this cause, and what solutions can you suggest?
tasks.zh: 主題：課堂錄影與現場聽課。問題與解決題：每個方法都要對應前面提出的困難。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
When institutions promote using recorded lectures for review, the change can cause practical difficulties for some people. The main problems become clear when the proposal meets different individual circumstances. A live review session gives students a chance to ask questions immediately. The teacher notices confusion and explains an idea in a different way. A recording alone does not answer a new question. Students also need a quiet place and a suitable device to use recordings. A person who cannot use the main arrangement may then miss a useful opportunity or need extra help to take part.

One solution is to improve the design and explain the available support clearly. Teachers can provide a short written outline with each recording. This supports students with limited internet access and makes the key points easier to find. A weekly question session adds interaction. The plan should explain which activities need attendance and which ones can be reviewed at home.

Another solution is to retain an appropriate alternative instead of assuming the main approach suits everyone. I support recordings as an extra resource. Live opportunities to ask questions should remain available, especially for difficult practical topics. This still allows the useful features of the proposal to remain. A recording allows a student to listen to an explanation again.

To sum up, recordings help students hear an explanation again, but they cannot answer a new question, and not everyone has a quiet place or a suitable device. A short written outline, a weekly question session and live help for difficult topics would let recordings support learning instead of replacing it.

tasks.prompt: Some people support digital vocabulary cards, while others favour paper vocabulary cards. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

tasks.sample:

For example, the learner checks the pronunciation of a nursing word before a speaking practice. The cards also fit into short breaks.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. Paper cards offer a simple activity without messages or other apps on the screen. A student can spread difficult cards across a desk and sort them by topic. A phone battery sometimes runs out during travel. Some learners also prefer writing a word with a pen.

Students can explain how they organise review and demonstrate a word in context. This keeps attention on learning. Requiring an expensive device would not prove that a learner understands the vocabulary.

To conclude, I think students should choose a method they use regularly. A small set of paper cards is also a useful backup for digital study. The best choice keeps the main benefits while making room for people whose circumstances are different from the majority.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring keeping a campus library open later over concentrating library services in daytime hours. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?
tasks.zh: 主題：延長圖書館時間與維持日間服務。分析優點和缺點；題目沒有要求哪邊較多，不必硬選輸贏。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
The proposal favouring keeping a campus library open later over concentrating library services in daytime hours raises questions about library opening hours. This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. Later opening hours give students another place to study after class. A nursing student with a daytime placement may reach campus in the evening. For example, the student uses a quiet desk to finish a reading task before returning to a shared dormitory room.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. Longer hours require staff, lighting and a safe way to enter the building. A nearly empty building still uses resources. Some students also need help from specialist library staff during the day. Moving resources to late hours could reduce support at the busiest times.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. The university can ask students when they need seats and compare demand across the week. A trial during examination periods is a useful starting point. Access arrangements and transport home need attention too. Decisions should reflect actual use instead of assuming every student follows the same timetable.

All things considered, I support a small late study area and clear daytime help hours. The whole library does not need identical opening times. Its benefits are real, but they only reach everyone when the limitations are planned for in advance and explained clearly.

tasks.prompt: Some people favour support from a student mentor, while others favour individual meetings with a teacher. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
tasks.zh: 主題：學長姐陪伴與教師個別協助。討論兩種看法並表達自己的意見。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
People have different views about peer mentoring. Some favour support from a student mentor, while others prefer individual meetings with a teacher. In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. A student mentor remembers the practical questions from the first year. A new student can ask where to find a classroom or how to prepare for a laboratory lesson. For example, a short campus tour makes the first week feel less confusing and starts a friendly conversation.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. A teacher understands formal course requirements and can deal with academic concerns. A student mentor may not know the answer to a complicated question. Personal experiences also differ. New students need a clear way to contact staff instead of treating another student's advice as an official rule.

A practical response should connect these arguments with the way the service or course actually works. The school can train mentors to say when they are unsure and explain where to refer a question. Meetings can be optional and short. Some students already have support outside school, while others need more help. A flexible system can respect both situations without leaving anyone isolated.

To sum up, I support student mentors for everyday guidance, with staff available for formal questions. The roles should be clear to everyone. Whatever the final decision is, it should be explained clearly so that people with different needs can still take part.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring writing a short reflection after each placement day over writing one longer reflection at the end of the week. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?
tasks.zh: 主題：每次寫反思與每週整理。分析優點和缺點；題目沒有要求哪邊較多，不必硬選輸贏。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
The proposal favouring writing a short reflection after each placement day over writing one longer reflection at the end of the week raises questions about clinical learning journals. This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. A short daily reflection helps a student remember a learning question. The learner records a general communication challenge without including patient details. For example, a student writes about feeling nervous during an introduction and practises a clearer opening sentence before the next day.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. A weekly reflection gives more time to connect several experiences. Students can compare their confidence at the start and end of a week. A long daily writing requirement adds work after a tiring day. Repeated summaries may also say little about the next learning step.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. Teachers can assess the quality of the learning plan rather than the number of pages. A clear question, an explanation and one next step are enough to guide a conversation. Institutions should explain privacy requirements and approved recording methods before students begin any placement reflection.

To conclude, I prefer a few private daily learning notes followed by one thoughtful weekly reflection. Patient information does not belong in personal study notes. Its advantages matter most when its limits are recognised and the people who need another option can still find one.

tasks.prompt: Some people support receiving comments after every writing exercise, while others favour receiving a weekly summary of writing feedback. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

tasks.sample:

In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. Quick comments help a learner connect feedback with a recent answer. The student still remembers the intended meaning and can try a correction at once. For example, a teacher points out one missing verb, and the learner rewrites the sentence before practising another example.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. A weekly summary can show a repeated difficulty across several exercises. The teacher has time to choose the most useful examples and explain one pattern carefully. Immediate comments on every line may feel overwhelming. Teachers also need time to prepare lessons and help other students.

A practical response should connect these arguments with the way the service or course actually works. Students can mark one sentence they are unsure about and bring it to a review session. The teacher can compare the first version with a later attempt. This shows whether the advice transfers to a new task. The timing should leave enough space for learners to think independently.

All things considered, I support quick feedback on the main problem and a weekly review of patterns. The aim is a usable next step, not a page full of corrections. Both views raise fair points, so the final arrangement should keep what works well on each side of the argument.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring more supervised simulation practice over more observation during clinical placements. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?

tasks.sample:
The proposal favouring more supervised simulation practice over more observation during clinical placements raises questions about simulation practice. This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. A simulation gives students a place to practise a defined task with a teacher. The group can pause and discuss a communication problem. For example, a student repeats an introduction to a simulated patient after feedback. The teacher can adjust the difficulty to the class.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. Clinical observation shows how staff work with real people in a busy setting. Students see different roles and hear questions that do not appear in a simple classroom script. Simulation equipment and teacher time also cost money. Neither setting can include every possible situation.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. A course team can map the purpose of each session before changing the timetable. Repeating a useful practice task may be better than adding a complicated new scenario. Students can explain what they learned afterwards. This helps teachers identify gaps without assuming that more hours alone guarantee better learning.

To sum up, I think both settings have a place. Students need preparation and supervision, with clear learning goals for simulation and placement activities. The approach works best when its limits are explained honestly and another reasonable option remains available to those who need it.

tasks.prompt: Some people support practising English with one regular partner, while others favour changing partners frequently. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

People have different views about English learning partners. Some support practising English with one regular partner, while others prefer changing partners frequently. In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. A regular partner becomes familiar with a learner's goals. The pair can notice progress and return to a difficult topic. For example, two nursing students practise introducing themselves in the first week and try a longer conversation later. A familiar person may make speaking feel easier.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. New partners bring different questions and speaking habits. A learner needs to understand more than one familiar voice. Working with the same person all term may also be difficult when schedules change. One student may talk much more than the other unless the activity is organised carefully.

A practical response should connect these arguments with the way the service or course actually works. Teachers can give partners equal speaking time and clear roles. A student can prepare a question before the meeting and record a general learning goal afterwards. Changing partners should not mean starting without support. Simple instructions help a quieter learner take part in either arrangement.

To conclude, I prefer a regular partner for some sessions and new partners for others. Both familiarity and variety are useful parts of speaking practice. A fair decision looks at the advantages and the costs together and offers a workable route for everyone involved.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring frequent full practice examinations over short practice tasks between occasional full examinations. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?
tasks.zh: 主題：頻繁模擬考與分段練習。分析優點和缺點；題目沒有要求哪邊較多，不必硬選輸贏。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
The proposal favouring frequent full practice examinations over short practice tasks between occasional full examinations raises questions about practice examinations. This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. A full practice examination lets students experience timing and several tasks together. A nursing student preparing for IELTS can notice how much time a long essay needs. For example, the student learns to leave a few minutes for checking rather than using the whole period on an introduction.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. Short tasks give learners time to work on one weakness. A student can practise writing an overview or developing a reason without completing a whole test. Frequent long examinations use much of the available study time. Repeating a test does not automatically explain why an answer needs improvement.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. A teacher can use a full test to identify two priorities and then design shorter follow-up tasks. Learners can compare a revised answer with their first attempt. This connects assessment with learning. The number of tests matters less than the opportunity to understand feedback and apply it later.

All things considered, I prefer focused practice most weeks and full examinations at planned intervals. The results should guide the next lesson instead of becoming the only activity. If its weaknesses are recognised early and handled sensibly, the advantages of this approach become much easier to keep.

tasks.sample:

In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. An oral presentation asks students to explain an idea clearly to listeners. Questions show which parts need another explanation. For example, a student introduces a community service in simple English and answers a classmate's question about its location. This creates practice for organised speaking.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. A written report allows more careful checking of sources and wording. Some subjects need detailed comparisons that are difficult to follow in a short talk. Presentations also take class time, and speaking anxiety can hide a student's understanding. The assessment needs a clear purpose.

A practical response should connect these arguments with the way the service or course actually works. Students can begin with a small-group talk before presenting to the whole class. A written outline can support the presentation without becoming a script read aloud. Teachers can assess content and delivery separately. Clear expectations help learners understand which part they need to improve next.

To sum up, I support both formats across a course. The format should match the skill being practised rather than forcing every assignment into the same form. A useful decision weighs the benefits against the limitations and explains how people with different circumstances can take part.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring following a fixed daily study timetable over adjusting study tasks each day. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?

This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. A fixed timetable reduces the number of decisions before studying. A learner knows when to open the vocabulary cards and when to write a short paragraph. For example, a student reviews English after breakfast on ordinary school days and develops a regular starting habit.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. Clinical placements, examinations and family responsibilities change the time available. A rigid timetable may become unrealistic during a busy week. Students also need more time for some topics than others. A plan should help organise work rather than create guilt about every unexpected change.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. A weekly plan can separate essential tasks from optional extra work. Students can check what they actually completed and adjust the next week. This makes the plan a useful record of learning. Teachers should avoid judging effort only by whether every learner studies at identical hours.

To conclude, I prefer a regular starting time with flexible task sizes. A smaller activity on a busy day can keep the routine realistic. The advantages are most useful when the limitations are acknowledged and there is a practical alternative for people who need it.

In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. Campus computers give students access to common software without requiring a new personal device. A learner can complete an assignment even when a home computer is unavailable. For example, a nursing student uses a library computer to format a presentation and check the course website.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. Personal devices allow students to work at convenient times and save their preferred settings. Campus rooms may be busy just before a deadline. Maintaining many shared computers also requires staff and money. Students still need accessible ways to use files and protect their account information.

The university can also offer loan equipment and clear instructions for signing out safely. Support should focus on the actual task. Buying more machines alone will not help if students cannot reach them when needed.

All things considered, I support dependable shared computers alongside personal devices. Access to coursework should not depend on owning an expensive machine. The best choice keeps the main benefits while making room for people whose circumstances are different from the majority.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring using only English during nursing language lessons over using Chinese explanations alongside English. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?

This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. English throughout a lesson gives learners repeated opportunities to listen and respond. Familiar classroom instructions become easier with practice. For example, students learn to ask for a word to be repeated and then use the same request during a conversation activity.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. A brief Chinese explanation can clarify a difficult meaning for a beginner. Without that support, a learner may repeat a sentence without understanding it. Nursing terms can be unfamiliar in both languages. A class also contains students with different levels of English experience.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. Teachers can introduce a simple English example, check comprehension and then choose whether translation is helpful. Students can explain the idea in their own words before returning to English. The amount of support can change as the course progresses, instead of following a rule that ignores learner readiness.

To sum up, I prefer mostly English practice with short Chinese explanations when needed. Understanding and active use should guide the choice of language. Its benefits are real, but they only reach everyone when the limitations are planned for in advance and explained clearly.

In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. One consistent model gives beginners a clear starting point. A learner can compare the same word across several practice sessions. For example, a nursing student listens to an introduction and copies its word stress before saying a personal version. This makes a short practice task manageable.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. English speakers do not all sound the same. Listening to different voices helps students prepare for unfamiliar speakers. A learner who only hears one recording may understand that recording well but struggle with a new one. The goal is clear communication, not an exact copy of one person.

A practical response should connect these arguments with the way the service or course actually works. A teacher can keep the vocabulary familiar while changing the speaker. Students can identify the main message first and then listen for details. This separates a new voice from a completely new topic. Pronunciation feedback should focus on understandable speech and useful practice rather than accent labels alone.

To conclude, I support a consistent starting model and gradual exposure to other voices. Students need both a clear example and opportunities to listen flexibly. Whatever the final decision is, it should be explained clearly so that people with different needs can still take part.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring joining a student club over using free time mainly for individual study. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?
tasks.zh: 主題：參加社團與專心課業。分析優點和缺點；題目沒有要求哪邊較多，不必硬選輸贏。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
The proposal favouring joining a student club over using free time mainly for individual study raises questions about student clubs. This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. A club gives students a reason to meet people outside their usual class. Members plan an activity and practise sharing responsibilities. For example, a nursing student joins an English club and helps arrange a short conversation game. The activity gives language study a social purpose.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. Students have different amounts of free time. Someone with paid work or a long journey home may find regular meetings difficult. A compulsory club can become another attendance requirement. Some students also prefer a small informal group or an activity outside the university.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. Universities can offer short introductory sessions and publish clear meeting times. They can also support occasional events for students unable to attend weekly meetings. Success should include whether participants feel welcome. A large membership list alone does not show that the activity fits students' needs.

All things considered, I think clubs should be easy to join but optional. Students need a choice of ways to meet people and develop interests. Its advantages matter most when its limits are recognised and the people who need another option can still find one.

When institutions promote joining a student club, the change can cause practical difficulties for some people. A new approach may be useful, but people differ in their access, experience and available time. This essay considers the problems and suggests ways to make the arrangement more workable.

The main problems become clear when the proposal meets different individual circumstances. Students have different amounts of free time. Someone with paid work or a long journey home may find regular meetings difficult. A compulsory club can become another attendance requirement. Some students also prefer a small informal group or an activity outside the university. A person who cannot use the main arrangement may then miss a useful opportunity or need extra help to take part.

One solution is to improve the design and explain the available support clearly. Universities can offer short introductory sessions and publish clear meeting times. They can also support occasional events for students unable to attend weekly meetings. Success should include whether participants feel welcome. A large membership list alone does not show that the activity fits students' needs.

Another solution is to retain an appropriate alternative instead of assuming the main approach suits everyone. I think clubs should be easy to join but optional. Students need a choice of ways to meet people and develop interests. This still allows the useful features of the proposal to remain. A club gives students a reason to meet people outside their usual class.

To sum up, clubs help students meet people, but compulsory membership ignores paid work, long journeys and different interests. Clubs that are easy to join but optional, with clear meeting times and occasional events for busy students, would welcome more people without adding another attendance rule.

tasks.prompt: Some people support taking a small part-time job during term, while others favour keeping term-time free for study. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
tasks.zh: 主題：學期中打工與保留讀書時間。討論兩種看法並表達自己的意見。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
People have different views about student paid work. Some support taking a small part-time job during term, while others prefer keeping term-time free for study. In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. Paid work gives students income and experience with schedules and customers. A student may use the income for transport or course materials. For example, a short weekend shift helps with ordinary expenses and provides practice in polite conversation with people from different backgrounds.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. Work hours can compete with study, rest and placement schedules. A late change in shifts may make planning difficult. Students also have different financial needs, so a simple rule does not fit everyone. Academic support should consider the whole timetable instead of assuming that every student has equal free time.

A practical response should connect these arguments with the way the service or course actually works. A school can publish placement dates early and explain where to request help. Employers can offer predictable shifts where possible. Students can review whether their current hours leave enough time for course requirements. Financial advice and hardship support are more useful than simply blaming learners for difficult choices.

To sum up, I prefer manageable work hours and early discussion of timetable conflicts. Students who need income should receive practical support. Both views raise fair points, so the final arrangement should keep what works well on each side of the argument.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring creating a shared dormitory study room over studying inside individual rooms. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?
tasks.zh: 主題：宿舍共用讀書區與房內讀書。分析優點和缺點；題目沒有要求哪邊較多，不必硬選輸贏。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。

The proposal favouring creating a shared dormitory study room over studying inside individual rooms raises questions about shared dormitory study space. This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. A separate study room gives residents a place for focused work. Roommates can keep different schedules without negotiating over every activity. For example, one nursing student reviews a lecture downstairs while another rests in their shared bedroom. Clear quiet rules make the purpose of the room easy to understand.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. A dormitory has limited space and residents need other shared facilities too. A study room may remain empty at some times and become crowded before examinations. Some students prefer a familiar desk in their own room. Access and fair use matter as much as the room itself.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. The dormitory can ask residents about demand before removing another facility. A small trial area may show which hours are useful. Clear rules for calls, food and leaving belongings can prevent conflict. Residents need a simple way to report problems and suggest changes to the arrangement.

To conclude, I support a shared quiet area with flexible opening hours. Residents should also agree on respectful ways to use their own rooms. The approach works best when its limits are explained honestly and another reasonable option remains available to those who need it.

tasks.prompt: Some people support offering optional weekend workshops, while others favour keeping all extra lessons on weekdays. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. A weekend workshop can provide a longer block of time for a focused activity. Students may be free from ordinary classes. For example, a nursing presentation workshop can include preparation, practice and feedback in one session instead of several short meetings during a crowded week.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. Weekends are also used for family visits, work and rest. Students with a long trip to campus may find an additional journey difficult. A workshop scheduled only on weekends excludes some learners. Staff also need predictable working arrangements and time to prepare the activity.

Short materials can support people who cannot attend, although practical activities still need suitable supervision. Publishing the purpose and expected workload early helps students decide which workshop fits their learning goals.

All things considered, I prefer a choice of times for optional workshops. A useful course should not assume that everyone is free on the same day. A fair decision looks at the advantages and the costs together and offers a workable route for everyone involved.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring frequent small quizzes over one extended course project. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?
tasks.zh: 主題：小考與學期專題。分析優點和缺點；題目沒有要求哪邊較多，不必硬選輸贏。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
The proposal favouring frequent small quizzes over one extended course project raises questions about course assessment. This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. Small quizzes give students regular information about their understanding. A learner notices a gap before moving to the next topic. For example, a short vocabulary quiz shows that a nursing student confuses two words, and the teacher uses a new sentence to explain the difference.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. A project allows students to connect ideas and develop an explanation over time. A quiz may measure recognition without showing how a learner uses information. Frequent tests can also take time away from discussion and feedback. Different course goals require different forms of evidence.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. Teachers can explain the purpose of each assessment before students start. A quiz result can lead to practice instead of only a score, while project feedback can include a chance to revise. Clear criteria make both formats more useful. No single method captures every part of a student's learning.

To sum up, I support several small checks and a meaningful project. The assessment should match the knowledge and skills taught in the course. If its weaknesses are recognised early and handled sensibly, the advantages of this approach become much easier to keep.

tasks.prompt: Some people support hospital maps on a phone, while others favour printed hospital visitor maps. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
tasks.zh: 主題：紙本導覽圖與手機導覽。討論兩種看法並表達自己的意見。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
People have different views about hospital visitor maps. Some support hospital maps on a phone, while others prefer printed hospital visitor maps. In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. A phone map can be updated when an entrance or service desk changes. Visitors can enlarge the text and carry the map without collecting paper. For example, a family member checks the route from the main entrance to a waiting area before arriving at the hospital.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. Not every visitor has a suitable phone or enough battery power. Some people find a printed map easier to read while asking a staff member for help. A mobile page may also be difficult to use with an unfamiliar language. Directions should remain available through several routes.

A practical response should connect these arguments with the way the service or course actually works. Hospitals can use matching names and symbols across signs, paper maps and digital pages. This reduces confusion when a visitor changes from one source to another. Feedback from actual visitors can identify unclear instructions. A simple map that people understand is more useful than a complicated feature list.

To conclude, I prefer a phone map with printed copies and staff assistance as alternatives. Visitors should be able to choose a practical format. A useful decision weighs the benefits against the limitations and explains how people with different circumstances can take part.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring booking clinic appointments online over booking appointments by telephone. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?

This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. Online booking lets a person check available times without waiting on a telephone line. A clear page can show the appointment details before confirmation. For example, a student compares several times after class and chooses one that does not conflict with a placement schedule.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. A telephone conversation allows a person to ask about unclear arrangements. Some users need help with digital forms or do not have reliable internet access. A booking page also needs clear instructions about its limits. It should not be treated as a way to assess urgent symptoms.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. A clinic can review where people leave an unfinished booking and simplify those steps. Confirmation messages should use clear language, with a way to correct a mistake. Staff need a process for helping people who cannot use the page. The aim is a workable appointment system for a broad range of users.

All things considered, I support online booking as an option with telephone assistance available. Access should not depend on digital confidence alone. The advantages are most useful when the limitations are acknowledged and there is a practical alternative for people who need it.

tasks.prompt: Some people support digital information screens in waiting areas, while others favour printed noticeboards in waiting areas. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. A digital screen can update information without replacing a sheet of paper. It can show a large heading and several language options. For example, a hospital uses it to explain the location of an information desk and the order of a non-clinical registration process.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. A changing display may move to the next page before a visitor finishes reading. Printed information stays visible and does not depend on power or a working screen. Some visitors also prefer to ask a person. Important directions need to be clear at the moment someone needs them.

A practical response should connect these arguments with the way the service or course actually works. Designers can test a notice with people unfamiliar with the building. A message can contain one main action instead of several paragraphs. Screen timing, text size and contrast all affect access. tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring booking hospital visits in advance over using fixed visiting periods without individual bookings. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?

The proposal favouring booking hospital visits in advance over using fixed visiting periods without individual bookings raises questions about hospital visiting arrangements. This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. Advance bookings can help staff understand how many visitors to expect. Families can discuss a suitable time before travelling. For example, relatives with different work hours arrange one planned visit rather than arriving together without knowing the local arrangements. Clear instructions can make preparation easier.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. A booking rule may be difficult for someone with unpredictable work or an unexpected family situation. Digital booking also creates a barrier for some visitors. Visiting arrangements need to consider the patient's wishes and the care setting. A single rule cannot explain every individual circumstance.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. Hospitals can explain the normal process and identify a contact for special circumstances. Families should know what to do if their planned time changes. The system should help communication rather than become a separate obstacle. Any proposal needs to recognise privacy, space and the work of the clinical team.

To conclude, I support clear visiting arrangements with a way to discuss exceptions. The patient's preferences and the unit's rules should guide the decision. Its benefits are real, but they only reach everyone when the limitations are planned for in advance and explained clearly.

tasks.prompt: Some people support short patient information in plain language, while others favour longer leaflets with detailed explanations. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

tasks.sample:

In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. Plain language makes the main message easier to follow. A clear heading and a familiar word can help a reader find the next step. For example, a visitor leaflet explains where to ask a question without using an unfamiliar department name or a long administrative phrase.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. Some information needs detail and careful explanation. Removing too much can leave a reader with unanswered questions. A short sentence is not automatically clear, especially when it contains an unexplained term. Readers also have different language and accessibility needs, so one version may not suit everyone.

A practical response should connect these arguments with the way the service or course actually works. A design team can ask readers to explain the main message in their own words. Their answers show which expressions need work. Appropriate translations and accessible formats may also be needed. A leaflet supports communication, but a person should still have a way to discuss a question with the relevant team.

All things considered, I prefer a clear short summary with further detail available. Writers should check understanding rather than count sentence length alone. Whatever the final decision is, it should be explained clearly so that people with different needs can still take part.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring one agreed family contact for routine updates over separate routine updates for several relatives. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?
tasks.zh: 主題：固定聯絡人與多人聯絡。分析優點和缺點；題目沒有要求哪邊較多，不必硬選輸贏。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
tasks.sample:
The proposal favouring one agreed family contact for routine updates over separate routine updates for several relatives raises questions about family communication. This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. An agreed contact can reduce repeated arrangements and help a family share general plans. For example, one relative coordinates visiting times and tells the others where to meet. Staff and families know whom to approach about practical matters, subject to the patient's permission and local rules.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. Family relationships differ, and one person may not be available or suitable for every conversation. Patients may have specific wishes about who receives information. A contact arrangement must not replace the patient's own voice. There also needs to be a way to change the arrangement when circumstances change.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. A team can explain the purpose of the contact and the limits of information sharing. It should record preferences using approved procedures, not informal personal notes. The arrangement needs review when the patient asks. Administrative convenience alone is not enough to decide who should receive personal information.

To sum up, I support discussing a contact arrangement with the patient rather than imposing one. Permission, privacy and flexibility are essential. Its advantages matter most when its limits are recognised and the people who need another option can still find one.

In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. A clear role label helps people know whom they are speaking with. A visitor can distinguish a nursing student from a qualified staff member. For example, a student introduces themselves and points to the role on the badge, making the introduction easier to follow.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. A badge also needs to follow the organisation's identification and safety rules. Making every detail large is not necessarily useful. Staff and students may have concerns about displaying unnecessary personal information. A clear spoken introduction still matters because some people cannot read the badge easily.

A practical response should connect these arguments with the way the service or course actually works. The hospital can ask patients, students and staff which information helps them identify roles. The badge should be easy to read without becoming crowded. Alternative ways to explain a role are also necessary. A uniform design is helpful only when the people using it understand the words and symbols.

To conclude, I support a readable role label and a spoken introduction. The design should follow local requirements and limit unnecessary personal details. Both views raise fair points, so the final arrangement should keep what works well on each side of the argument.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring staff English conversation groups over individual online English practice. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?

tasks.sample:

This approach offers practical advantages, but it also has limitations. Both sides need consideration because an arrangement that works well for one person may be less suitable for another.

One important advantage concerns the way people can carry out the activity. A conversation group gives staff a chance to practise speaking with colleagues. Members can rehearse ordinary introductions using fictional situations. For example, a short session practises asking someone to repeat a general question. Shared practice can also reveal common language-learning needs.

There are also disadvantages that the proposal should address. Staff work different shifts and may not be free at one meeting time. Individual online practice offers flexibility and a chance to repeat a difficult sentence privately. A conversation group also needs a clear purpose and appropriate support. It should not replace qualified language assistance for actual patient communication.

These disadvantages do not mean that the proposal has no value, but they affect how it should be organised. Organisers can offer short sessions at several times and use invented scenarios without patient details. Participants can choose one useful language goal. Attendance should not become a substitute for checking communication needs in practice. Training is most useful when its limits and its intended learning outcomes are clear.

All things considered, I support optional groups alongside individual resources. Real communication needs should follow the hospital's approved language-support procedures. The approach works best when its limits are explained honestly and another reasonable option remains available to those who need it.

tasks.prompt: Some people support placements at a wider range of locations, while others favour fewer placement locations with stable travel. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

In my opinion, the choice should depend on the purpose and the needs of the people involved. Neither option needs to become the only acceptable approach in every situation.

Supporters of the first option have several reasons for their view. Different settings can show students a range of working environments and team arrangements. A learner compares how introductions and information sessions are organised. For example, a student sees a community setting and a larger hospital, then discusses the learning differences with a teacher.

However, the alternative also deserves attention. Frequent location changes add travel costs and preparation time. Students need to learn each site's layout, rules and supervision arrangements. A stable placement can provide time to develop confidence with one team. More locations do not automatically mean that the learning experiences are better.

It can then explain travel arrangements and provide orientation before the move. Students should have a way to raise access difficulties early. The decision should balance variety with continuity rather than treating the number of sites as the main measure.

To sum up, I prefer a planned range of placements with enough time at each site. Travel and supervision need consideration before adding another location. A fair decision looks at the advantages and the costs together and offers a workable route for everyone involved.

To conclude, I support online preparation followed by an in-person orientation. Each part should have a clear purpose and a way to ask questions. If its weaknesses are recognised early and handled sensibly, the advantages of this approach become much easier to keep.

tasks.prompt: Consider a proposal favouring several smaller local information points over a large central public information centre. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this proposal?
tasks.zh: 主題：集中服務與社區據點。分析優點和缺點；題目沒有要求哪邊較多，不必硬選輸贏。至少250字，提出解釋與具體例子；範文是練習示範，不代表保證取得某個雅思級分。
